title: Nobody Believes a Barefoot Boy
part: PART THREE: WHAT THE MOUNTAIN KNEW

pages.text:
*From the Walk-Book of Highstep, Day 20. Weather: cloud. Distance: three miles. Direction: left. The village has been told. The village has views.*

The cheese crate was wobbly, which was the first bad sign. The second was that Mo’s hands were shaking so hard the paper rustled, sounding like a dry leaf in a gale. He stood up, his bare feet gripping the wooden slats, and held the brittle page out in front of him. It looked fragile, as if a strong breath might turn it to dust.

"Tor is old," he said. His voice cracked on the second word. He cleared his throat, pressed one heel hard against the crate, and tried again. "She is very old. And she is walking to the Gathering."

A silence fell, heavy and thick.

"She will rest there," Mo continued, his eyes scanning the sea of faces. "She will lie down. And Highstep will stay. We will not walk anymore."

Nobody cheered. Nobody clapped. A woman near the front, holding a bundle of mending, simply stared at him as if he had grown a second head. Mo lowered his arms, the page trembling between his fingers.
pages.image: Mo stands on a wooden cheese crate, holding a small brittle paper page with both hands, his bare feet gripping the slats, while a crowd of villagers in wool and aprons watches him with wide, confused eyes in a pine-forested clearing.

pages.text:
A low murmur rippled through the crowd, starting near the back and moving forward like water over stones. Someone laughed, a short, sharp bark, and then another voice joined in, softer this time.

"Children's tales," said a farmer, shaking his head. "My grandfather said the same thing before the cheese caves flooded. Do not credit the barefoot boy with a mountain’s mind."

Mama Achebe stepped forward. Her face was tight, but kind. She did not look angry. She looked tired, the kind of tired that comes from weaving too many patterns in one day.

"I have no room in my heart today for one more story, Mo," she said gently. "We have cheese to make and ropes to mend. Please."

Mayor Marsh adjusted her green sash. She did not scold. She simply nodded, her clipboard clutched to her chest.

"I am grateful you tried," she said, her voice brisk and official. "But a village cannot be planned around a page that could have been written by anyone."

Mo felt the ground beneath the crate tilt, just slightly, as if Tor herself was shrugging.
pages.image: A round woman in a tall hat and green sash holds a clipboard, speaking calmly to a small boy on a crate, while a tired woman in an apron looks on with a pained, gentle expression amidst a crowd of villagers.

pages.text:
Gran stood up. She was so small next to the other adults that she seemed to vanish into the crowd, but her voice did not. It cut through the murmur, sharp and clear as the bell on her staff.

"The page is real," she said.

The quiet that followed was different. It was not the quiet of disbelief. It was the quiet of a held breath, of a room where everyone is waiting to see if the floor will give way.

"Stepkeeper," Mayor Marsh said, her voice dropping. "Gran."

"Ada," said a man from the rope guild, his arms crossed. "You are seventy-three. Your eyes are bad. You write in a book for the fun of it. How do we know this is not another one of your... games?"

Mo looked at his father. Tomás stood with his back to the crowd, his large hands resting on his rope coil. He was whistling through his teeth, a low, tuneless sound. He did not turn around. He did not look at Mo. The silence of his father was louder than any shout, and it settled in Mo’s chest like a stone.
pages.image: A tiny old woman with a long white braid and huge spectacles stands firmly in a crowd, while a large man with a rope coil over his shoulder turns his back, whistling, and a small boy watches him with a hurt expression.

pages.text:
The argument did not end with a verdict. It ended with a count. Mayor Marsh began to tally the families on her clipboard, and the number of those who wanted to descend at the Last Ladder grew by the minute. It was a slow, quiet tide, pulling people away from the future.

Mo looked around for Junie. He expected to see her, tall and stubborn, arguing or defending. But her spot in the crowd was empty. The yellow scarf that usually bobbed above the heads was gone.

He climbed down from the crate, his legs unsteady. He walked to the Footpost, the flat stone in the center of the Green, where he had stood every morning of his life. There, resting on the stone, was her scrapbook. It was open.

Inside, tucked between a drawing of a square window and a sketch of a straight horizon, was a note. The handwriting was sharp and slanted.

I am not leaving you. I am leaving the tilt.

Mo picked up the book. It was warm, as if she had just set it down. He closed his eyes and pressed his bare heel to the stone. Under his foot, Tor was walking. Steady. Patient. Unwavering.
pages.image: A small boy stands alone on a flat stone, holding an open sketchbook with a piece of paper inside, his bare feet planted firmly, while the empty space around him suggests a crowd has moved away, with pine trees in the background.

pages.text:
Words were light things. They scattered on the wind like loose leaves. Seeing was different. Seeing was heavy, like a stone you could hold.

Mo needed the crowd to see. He turned to the rope store. A coil of thick hemp waited on the shelf. The fibers were rough against his palms. He took a lantern from the hook. The glass was clean. From the bakery table, he grabbed a heel of stale bread. It was hard enough to last two days.

He shouldered the rope. The lantern went into his poncho. He bit into the bread.

Admiral was already there. His tin bell jingled softly as he chewed a piece of straw. The goat did not look at Mo. He did not ask where they were going. He simply lifted one ear. Then he stepped forward, waiting for Mo to follow.
pages.image: A small boy with a green poncho carries a coil of rope and a lantern, eating a heel of bread, while a large brown and white goat with one crooked horn stands patiently beside him, looking forward toward a dark pine forest.
